chapters.desc: The poem opens, as the Book of Allah does, in His name, then praises Allah as the Possessor of dominion, might and authority, and sends blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ, the one who governed by the Qur’an. The attributes are chosen to harmonize with the subject of the poem, an art the scholars of balāghah call barāʿat al-istihlāl, the eloquence of introduction.

verses.tr: All praise to Allah, mighty and supreme, whose authority, power, and rule encompass every scheme.

exp.en:
About the poet

Dr Waleed ibn Idrīs al-Manīsī was born in Alexandria, Egypt, and currently resides in Minnesota, USA. He serves as a senior member of the Permanent Fatwa Committee of the Assembly of Muslim Jurists of America (AMJA), Vice President of the Islamic University of Minnesota, Imam and Chairman of the Dar al-Farooq Islamic Centre, and a member of the North American Imams Federation (NAIF).

He obtained his bachelor’s degree in Arabic Language from Alexandria University, his master’s degree in Islamic jurisprudence from the American Open University (summa cum laude), and his PhD from the Graduate Theological Foundation.

Dr Waleed studied under prominent scholars including Shaykh Ibn Bāz, Shaykh Ibn ʿUthaymīn and Shaykh Ibn Jibrīn, and received tazkiyāt (recommendations) from Shaykh ʿAbd al-Razzāq ʿAfīfī and Shaykh Ṣāliḥ al-Shaykh.

He memorized the Qur’an in the ten canonical recitations through al-Shāṭibiyyah, al-Durrah and al-Ṭayyibah, and mastered the four anomalous (shawādh) recitations as well. His ijāzāt in Qur’anic recitation trace back through one of the shortest chains to the Prophet ﷺ.

Among his works are:

  • Rules of Proving and Seeing the New Moons (PhD dissertation)
  • The Impact of Qirāʾāt Variations on Creed and Jurisprudence (Master’s thesis)
  • Summary of al-Ṣirāṭ al-Mustaqīm
  • Fatwas and Biography of Shaykh ʿAbd al-Razzāq ʿAfīfī
  • Poetry on Islamic Inheritance Laws
  • Poetry on the Science of Qur’anic Recitation
  • Ittiḥāf al-Ṣuḥbah bi-Riwāyat Shuʿbah (didactic poem)
  • Judicial Work Outside the Islamic State

The opening lines

  1. Begin with the Name of Allah: following the example set by the Book of Allah.
  2. Praise of Allah: acknowledgment of His greatness.
  3. Salutations upon the Prophet ﷺ: respect for his guidance.

Beginning with the Name of Allah

The opening with Bismillāh al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm follows the example set by the Book of Allah, which begins with this noble phrase, and the letters of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who would begin his correspondence with it.

It is reported that when he wrote to Heraclius, the Emperor of Rome, he began by saying:

بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ، مِنْ مُحَمَّدٍ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ إِلَى هِرَقْلَ عَظِيمِ الرُّومِ…

“Bismillāh al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm. From Muḥammad, the Messenger of Allah, to Heraclius, the Great of the Romans…” Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim

This establishes a prophetic precedent that every matter of importance should begin in the name of Allah, a reminder of his saying ﷺ:

كُلُّ أَمْرٍ ذِيْ بَالٍ لَا يُبْدَأُ فِيْهِ بِبِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِيْمِ فَهُوَ أَبْتَرُ

“Every significant affair that is not begun with the name of Allah is cut off (abtar).”

Thus, beginning this discussion on al-Siyāsah al-Sharʿiyyah (Islamic Legal-Political Theory) with the basmalah is not merely a formal opening, but a spiritual orientation, seeking Allah’s guidance, blessing and rectitude in exploring one of the most delicate and consequential fields of the Sharīʿah.

Praise of Allah, the Possessor of Majesty and Sovereignty

It is fitting that the author begins with the praise of Allah, exalted in His Majesty, recognizing His supreme greatness (ʿaẓamah) and that He alone is the Possessor of dominion (dhū al-mulk), might (al-quwwah) and authority (al-sulṭān).

This opening aligns beautifully with the subject matter of the verses, a demonstration of what scholars of balāghah call barāʿat al-istihlāl (the eloquence of introduction): the art of selecting attributes of Allah that harmonize with the subject of the discourse.

Here, the chosen attributes, al-mulk, al-quwwah and al-sulṭān, align seamlessly with the theme of as-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah, which deals with governance, authority and rule. The poet reminds us that every form of power or dominion in this world exists only by Allah’s permission.

Thus, every form of governance, rule and leadership discussed under the study of as-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah ultimately derives from His will, His granting and His wisdom.

verses.tr: Then blessings and peace, eternal and true, upon the chosen Prophet, Muhammad ﷺ, too.

exp.en:
Salutations upon the Prophet ﷺ

The author then sends peace and blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ, employing the phrase السَّرْمَدِيّ, a term that conveys continuity and eternity. Linguistically, as-sarmadī means perpetual, everlasting, without beginning or end (dāʾim alladhī lā bidāyata lahu).

By using this expression, the poet wishes that salutations upon the Prophet ﷺ be continuous and unceasing, a reflection of his timeless honor and the enduring relevance of his message.

The Prophet ﷺ is also described as الْمُصْطَفَى, the Chosen One (alladhī ikhtārahu Allāhu ʿazza wa-jall wa faḍḍalahu): the one whom Allah selected and elevated above all creation. These two expressions, as-sarmadī and al-muṣṭafā, together encapsulate both the eternal continuity of the Prophet’s honor and the divine selection that defines his station.

They serve as a refined literary and spiritual prelude, reminding the reader that every discussion within as-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah ultimately traces its legitimacy and light back to the Prophet ﷺ, the divinely chosen guide for all aspects of life: spiritual, moral and political.

verses.tr: He who governed by the Qur’an, the best of nations, and guided the people with the finest of regulations.

exp.en:
The one who governed by the Qur’an

The poet then praises the Prophet ﷺ through the very quality that defines the subject of the poem: his just and divinely guided governance.

“The one who governed the best of nations through the Qur’an, and reformed people through the finest of laws.”

Here, the Prophet ﷺ is portrayed as the supreme model of leadership (sās bi’l-Qur’ān), who reformed society not through worldly power, but through revelation and divine justice.

This too reflects barāʿat al-istihlāl, the eloquence of introduction, wherein the author harmonizes his opening praise with the central theme of his composition. By aligning the Prophet’s attributes with as-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah, the poet establishes that true governance and societal reform can only emerge through the guidance of the Qur’an and the Sunnah of its bearer ﷺ.

These profound meanings, the remembrance of Allah’s majesty, the eternal salutations upon His Chosen Messenger ﷺ and the acknowledgment of his just leadership, are what the poet beautifully captures in his opening lines.

chapters.desc: As-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah is the system through which the higher objectives of the Sharīʿah are realized, and its science is one of immense significance; yet few have ever set it into verse. Having sought Allah’s guidance through istikhārah, the poet sets out to gather the chapters of this science in one manẓūmah.

verses.tr: Next comes governance within the sacred law, where religion’s aims are nurtured and held in awe.

exp.en:
The purpose and scope of as-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah

As-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah is the system through which the Maqāṣid ash-Sharīʿah, the higher objectives of the Divine Law, are realized. These objectives revolve around securing benefit (jalb al-maṣlaḥah) and repelling harm (dafʿ al-mafsadah) in both religion and worldly life.

Or, as the scholars have expressed it:

“To attain the welfare of both this world and the Hereafter, and to repel harm in both realms.”

The classical scholars have identified five essential objectives (al-ḍarūriyyāt al-khamsah) that the Sharīʿah came to preserve:

  1. Preservation of religion (ḥifẓ ad-dīn)
  2. Preservation of life (ḥifẓ an-nafs)
  3. Preservation of intellect (ḥifẓ al-ʿaql)
  4. Preservation of wealth (ḥifẓ al-māl)
  5. Preservation of honor and dignity (ḥifẓ al-ʿirḍ)

Through as-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah, these divine objectives find their practical realization in governance, law and public order, ensuring that leadership in Islam serves as a means of mercy, justice and protection for humanity in both worlds.

It is important to note, as Mufti Muhammad Taqi Usmani elaborates:

“At the same time, Islam does not dictate a rigid, unchanging form of government. It lays down principles, not blueprints. The Qur’an and Sunnah provide enduring guidance, justice, consultation (shūrā), accountability and the protection of rights, while leaving the detailed structure of governance to the wisdom of scholars and leaders of each age.

This balance between fixed principles and flexible application is what gives as-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah its timeless relevance. The unchanging goals of justice and mercy remain constant, even as their practical forms adapt to time and place.” Usmani, M.T., Islam and Politics, Turath Publications, 2018, pp. 26–27

These meanings, that political order in Islam is a means of fulfilling the higher purposes of the Sharīʿah and not an end, are beautifully expressed by the poet in this concise verse.

verses.tr: Its science is one of lofty worth, yet few have ever set it into verse.

exp.en:
The purpose of this poem

ʿIlm as-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah, the science of Islamic moral and legal governance, is one of immense significance and elevated standing within the Sharīʿah. It is the bridge between knowledge and leadership, theory and application, revelation and policy.

Such a science deserves to be studied, taught and internalized with the same reverence afforded to other core Islamic disciplines. Yet, despite its depth and relevance, the author laments how rarely it has been treated poetically:

“Few have ever composed poetry on this subject.”

Only a handful of scholars, he notes, have ever ventured to capture its discussions in verse, and even then, their works were confined to particular chapters or select themes:

“Each of them confined their work to only certain chapters or selected aspects of the subject.”

Thus, there is a gap in the scholarly tradition. The science, though grand in scope, has not been fully versified in a way that renders its principles both memorable and aesthetically engaging. So the author justifies the very purpose of his composition: to present as-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah not only as a theoretical and juristic field but as one worthy of poetic articulation, thereby making its principles accessible, memorable and engaging to students of both fiqh and adab.

verses.tr: So, I sought Allah’s guidance in composing these lines, gathering within them the chapters of this noble science.

exp.en:
Having established the worth of the discipline, the author next reveals the spirit in which he began his composition, one of humility and reliance upon Allah. Before writing this poem, he performed istikhārah, seeking divine guidance and blessing in what he was about to undertake.

This invocation of istikhārah situates the poem within the ethical and spiritual ethos of Islamic scholarship, where every act of teaching or authorship begins with conscious surrender to Allah’s will. It reflects the belief that intellectual success is not merely a result of diligence, but of tawfīq, divine enablement.

Moreover, his intention to compose a manẓūmah that “encompasses the chapters of this science” shows his aspiration to present as-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah in a comprehensive and structured form, one that gathers its major discussions, principles and objectives into a cohesive poetic framework.

That is what the poet expresses in these lines: his reliance upon Allah, transforming his project from a literary exercise into an act of worship. His intent is not merely to compose, but to serve: to produce a work that benefits, inspires and revives attention toward an often-overlooked branch of sacred knowledge.

chapters.desc: Every science has ten starting points (al-mabādiʾ al-ʿasharah) that give an overview of the field, its nature and its intended purpose. In eight abyāt the poet applies them to as-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah: its definition, subject, benefit, virtue, relation, founder, name, sources, ruling and issues.

verses.tr: In technical terminology, siyāsah is defined as: the proper management of the state’s affairs.

exp.en:
The ten foundational principles of as-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah

Every science has a set of starting points (mabādiʾ), which serve as the introductory premises (muqaddimāt). There are ten such principles for this discipline. It is beneficial when studying any science to present these principles at the outset, as they provide a general overview of the field, its nature and its intended purpose.

Scholars have summarized this in ten foundational principles, known as al-Mabādiʾ al-ʿAsharah, “the Ten Principles”:

  1. Definition: the clear explanation of the science.
  2. Subject: the focus of the science.
  3. Benefit: the outcomes or benefits of the science.
  4. Relation: the connections to other fields.
  5. Merit: the value or importance of the science.
  6. Founder: the originator of the science.
  7. Name: the title or label of the science.
  8. Sources: the origins of the science’s knowledge.
  9. Ruling of the Sharīʿah: the alignment with Islamic law.
  10. Issues: the challenges or problems in the science.

Imam al-Ṣabbān beautifully captured them in verse:

إن مبادئ كل علم عشرة ۞ الحدّ والموضوع ثم الثمرة

ونسبته وفضله والواضع ۞ والاسم والاستمداد حُكم الشارع

مسائلٌ والبعضُ بالبعض اكتفى ۞ ومن دَرى الجميع حاز الشرفا

The principles of every science are ten:
its definition, its subject, then its fruit;
its relation, its merit, and its founder;
its name, its sources, and the ruling of the Sharīʿah;
its issues. Some suffice with a few of these,
but whoever knows them all attains distinction and honor.

These ten principles serve as a roadmap for every student of knowledge. Let us look at how they apply to as-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah.

1. Definition (al-ḥadd)

Linguistically (لغة): the word siyāsah derives from the root sāsa, as in the expression ساس القوم: he governed or held authority over the people. This conveys the sense of taking charge, ruling, or being responsible for the people.

Technically (اصطلاحًا): the technical meaning does not depart from the linguistic sense. As-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah refers to any action or policy that brings people closer to righteousness and keeps them away from corruption, as defined by Ibn ʿAqīl:

السياسة: ما كان من الأفعال بحيث يكون الناسُ أقربَ إلى الصلاح وأبعد عن الفساد

“As-siyāsah is that course of action by which people are brought nearer to rectitude and kept farther from corruption.”

The term “ash-Sharʿiyyah” indicates that such governance is bound by the Qur’an and Sunnah, meaning the ruler manages the affairs of the state only through what aligns with revelation and never in opposition to it.

Thus, as-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah retains its linguistic essence of authority and leadership, but its scope is religiously guided, deriving legitimacy and purpose from the Sharīʿah, as this verse reflects.

ajuzW.g: and what is due from him

verses.tr: Its subject is the rights of every ruler known, and all their conditions and duties, let these clearly be shown.

exp.en:
2. Subject (al-mawḍūʿ)

The subject of ʿIlm as-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah encompasses the laws, governance structures and regulations that ensure the well-being of the people in both religion and worldly affairs. It defines:

  1. Rights of the ruler (حقوق كل حاكم): the obedience and support owed to rulers when they govern justly and in accordance with the Sharīʿah.
  2. Conditions (شروطه): the prerequisites for assuming or dismissing office, and related governance conditions.
  3. Duties of the ruler (ما عليه): the responsibilities incumbent upon rulers toward their people, including justice, protection of rights, and promotion of welfare.

Scholarly works have approached this subject from multiple angles:

  • Financial governance: managing public funds, sources of revenue (bayt al-māl) and proper distribution, exemplified in Imam Abū Yūsuf’s book al-Kharāj and Abū ʿUbaid al-Qāsim ibn Sallām’s Kitāb al-Amwāl.
  • International relations: guidance for rulers in matters of peace, war and diplomacy, ensuring the welfare of the Muslim community. This area became known as ʿilm as-siyar (distinct from ʿilm al-sīrah, the Prophet’s biography), with early contributions from Imam al-Awzāʿī and Imam Muhammad ibn al-Ḥasan.
  • Regulation of non-Muslims (aḥkām ahl al-dhimmah): rules governing non-Muslim residents in an Islamic state, as discussed by Ibn al-Qayyim رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ.
  • Practical governance and justice: employing discernment (al-fatānah) and wisdom to maximize public benefit, regulate punishments, and apply discretionary measures (taʿzīr) to uphold justice, as outlined in works like Ibn Taymiyyah’s رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ al-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah and Ibn al-Qayyim’s رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ al-Ṭuruq al-Ḥikmiyyah fī as-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah.

A practical illustration is provided by the Prophet ﷺ through the story reported by Abū Hurayrah:

عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ، أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ ﷺ قَالَ: «كَانَتِ امْرَأَتَانِ مَعَهُمَا ابْنَاهُمَا، جَاءَ الذِّئْبُ فَذَهَبَ بِابْنِ إِحْدَاهُمَا، فَقَالَتْ لِصَاحِبَتِهَا: إِنَّمَا ذَهَبَ بِابْنِكِ، وَقَالَتِ الْأُخْرَى: إِنَّمَا ذَهَبَ بِابْنِكِ، فَتَحَاكَمَتَا إِلَى دَاوُدَ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ فَقَضَى بِهِ لِلْكُبْرَى، فَخَرَجَتَا عَلَى سُلَيْمَانَ بْنِ دَاوُدَ عَلَيْهِمَا السَّلَامُ فَأَخْبَرَتَاهُ، فَقَالَ: ائْتُونِي بِالسِّكِّينِ أَشُقُّهُ بَيْنَهُمَا، فَقَالَتِ الصُّغْرَى: لَا تَفْعَلْ يَرْحَمُكَ اللَّهُ، هُوَ ابْنُهَا، فَقَضَى بِهِ لِلصُّغْرَى»

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Two women came, each with her child. A wolf came and took one of the children. One woman said to the other, ‘It is only your child that was taken,’ while the other said, ‘It is only your child that was taken.’ They went to Dāwūd عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ for judgment, and he initially ruled in favor of the elder woman. Then they went to Sulaymān ibn Dāwūd عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ and informed him of the case. He said, ‘Bring me a knife so I may divide the child between them.’ The younger woman said, ‘Do not do so, may Allah have mercy on you; he is her child.’ He then gave the child to the younger woman.”

Ibn al-Qayyim رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ comments on this case, noting that the judgment prioritized the clear evidence and the observable circumstance: the elder mother’s consent and the younger mother’s protective concern were weighed, demonstrating the ruler’s use of discernment and the consideration of contextual evidence (qarāʾin ẓāhirah) in decision-making.

This example illustrates the practical application of ʿIlm as-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah: rulers must balance rights, conditions and duties to ensure justice and public welfare.

verses.tr: The benefits of this knowledge are the way to attain, a rule by God’s law, just and plain.

exp.en:
3. Benefit (ath-thamarah)

The benefit of this discipline is the application of Sharīʿah governance in society, ensuring justice prevails and the higher objectives of the law are realized. As the author states:

“To employ this knowledge to establish the rule of the Sharīʿah and to apply Allah’s law among the people, so that justice is implemented in society.”

In other words, the practical outcome of mastering this discipline is the realization of divine governance on earth, ensuring that:

  1. The Sharīʿah is implemented in rulings and governance.
  2. Justice prevails in dealings between people.
  3. Society is guided toward both worldly and spiritual well-being, aligning human authority with divine objectives.

This underscores that as-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah is not an abstract theoretical science; its benefit lies in its practical application, directly affecting governance, public order and societal justice under the framework of Islamic law.

verses.tr: Its virtue is the same as the virtue of knowledge in general, and to Fiqh it belongs, O’ the forbearing one.

exp.en:
4. Virtue (al-faḍl)

“The merit of this science lies in its inclusion within the general excellence of knowledge.”

Some disciplines have specific merits mentioned explicitly in the Sunnah or Qur’ān, with texts highlighting their unique virtues. However, for this science there is no direct, specific evidence of its merit. Instead, it is encompassed within the general excellence of knowledge in Islam, as indicated by the āyah:

﴿وَقُلْ رَبِّ زِدْنِي عِلْمًا﴾

“And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge.” Ṭā Hā 20:114

Thus, while as-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah may not have unique ḥadīth or Qur’anic texts praising it separately, it shares in the overall virtue of the Islamic sciences, which aim to benefit humanity and establish divine guidance.

5. Relation (an-nisbah)

“Its relation is to fiqh.”

Siyāsah sharʿiyyah is part of the broader field of Islamic jurisprudence, drawing upon its principles, foundations and methodologies. It is considered a sub-branch or applied aspect of fiqh, because it addresses topics such as:

  • Jihād: regulations regarding defence and struggle
  • Collection and distribution of wealth
  • Rulings concerning non-Muslim residents
  • Punishments and discretionary penalties

Therefore, the science derives its legitimacy, methodology and principles from fiqh, while focusing on the governance and welfare of society in accordance with the objectives of the Sharīʿah.

It is important to note, as Mufti Muhammad Taqi Usmani explains in his book Islam and Politics, that:

“Politics occupies an important place in religion, but to declare it the principal purpose of religion would upset the broader system of priorities. Likewise, to limit religion solely to prayer and fasting while neglecting its other branches would be a mistake. Religion encompasses many branches, and politics is one of them. To live according to Islam, all injunctions must be acted upon, whichever branch they belong to.

In practice, individuals may dedicate themselves to one branch, such as politics, applying their efforts there sincerely for the sake of serving Islam and the Muslims, without assuming it to be the sole purpose of religion.” Usmani, M.T., Islam and Politics, Turath Publications, 2018, p. 25

verses.tr: Its founder is the companion of al-Nuʿmān (Imām Abū Ḥanīfah), and its compiler is al-Māwardī, the man of mastery.

exp.en:
6. Founder (al-wāḍiʿ)

“Its founder is the one known as Ṣāḥib an-Nuʿmān.”

The discipline was pioneered by Ṣāḥib an-Nuʿmān. Here, Ṣāḥib an-Nuʿmān (the companion of al-Nuʿmān) refers to Imām Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb ibn Ibrāhīm al-Anṣārī, better known as al-Qāḍī Abū Yūsuf, who was one of the two foremost students of Imām Abū Ḥanīfah (al-Nuʿmān ibn Thābit).

Abū Yūsuf served as judge under Caliph Hārūn al-Rashīd and authored Kitāb al-Kharāj, a seminal work addressing the financial administration of the Islamic state, including taxation, revenue, and the ruler’s responsibilities toward the people.

The other leading student of Abū Ḥanīfah, Imām Muḥammad al-Shaybānī, wrote Kitāb as-Siyar, which focuses on international relations, the rules of peace (salām) and war (ḥarb), and other matters relevant to governance and diplomacy.

The comprehensive compiler: al-Māwardī

“The one who first compiled the matters of this science comprehensively is Imām al-Māwardī, known for his mastery.”

Al-Qāḍī Abū al-Ḥasan al-Māwardī (Shāfiʿī, died 450 AH) was the first scholar to bring together all the chapters and issues of this science into a single, systematic work. His book, al-Aḥkām as-Sulṭāniyyah, organizes the laws of governance according to the Shāfiʿī school, covering both administrative and judicial matters comprehensively.

Prior works, while valuable, did not encompass all aspects of the science, leaving gaps that al-Māwardī sought to fill.

This section thus establishes both the pioneers of siyāsah sharʿiyyah, Abū Yūsuf and al-Shaybānī, and its first comprehensive compiler, al-Māwardī, highlighting the evolution of the discipline from practical rulings and partial studies to a systematic, all-encompassing science.

verses.tr: Its name is As-Siyāsah Ash-Sharʿiyyah. Likewise, it is known as Al-Ahkām As-Sultāniyyah.

exp.en:
7. Name of this science (al-ism)

Some sciences have more than one name. Similarly, this discipline is known by two widely recognized titles:

  1. As-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah (السياسة الشرعية)
    • This title emphasizes the application of the Sharīʿah in governance and administration.
    • Classical works under this title include al-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah by Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah and another by Ibn al-Qayyim رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ تَعَالَى.
  2. Al-Aḥkām as-Sulṭāniyyah (الأحكام السلطانية)
    • This title highlights the legal rulings related to authority, leadership and statecraft.
    • Classical works under this title include al-Aḥkām as-Sulṭāniyyah by al-Māwardī and another by Abū Yaʿlā رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ تَعَالَى.

Note: the word سلطانية is presented in the indefinite form (nākirah) solely for metrical purposes in the poetry.

This distinction of names reflects the scope and focus of the science, and it is what this verse captures.

verses.tr: It is supported by the two foundations (Qur’ān and Sunnah), then by the Prophet’s way, and by the Rightly Guided Caliphs, a model to display.

exp.en:
8. Sources (al-istimdād)

Just as other sciences may be derived from language, principles or other sources, ʿIlm as-Siyāsah ash-Sharʿiyyah draws its authority and content from two primary foundations:

  1. The Qur’an: the ultimate source of divine law and guidance.
  2. The Sunnah: specifically the Prophet’s ﷺ Seerah (life and conduct), including his military expeditions and social dealings.

In addition to these comes the example set by the four Rightly Guided Caliphs, who are highlighted as models of just and effective governance.

Thus, the sources of this science are:

  • Divine revelation (Qur’an and Sunnah) for legal and moral foundations.
  • Practical precedent (Seerah and the governance of the Rāshidūn) for implementation, policy and administration.

This principle emphasises that siyāsah sharʿiyyah is firmly rooted in divine revelation and brought to life through the actions of the Prophet and the Rightly Guided Caliphs. It ensures that governance is not just a matter of abstract theory but is guided by both the aims of the Sharīʿah and the practical needs of society.

verses.tr: Its ruling is a collective obligation (farḍ kifāyah), and its masāʾil (issues) are outlined in the chapters of this poem.

exp.en:
9. Ruling (ḥukm)

Studying and teaching this science is farḍ kifāyah, a communal obligation. This means that if some members of the community acquire and teach this knowledge, the sin is lifted from the rest. However, part of the Ummah must undertake learning and teaching this science, so that society benefits from proper understanding and implementation of siyāsah sharʿiyyah.

Thus, studying and transmitting this science is not merely recommended; it is an essential duty for the community’s welfare and the proper application of the Sharīʿah.

10. Masāʾil (issues)

“The issues of this science are organized into the chapters of this manẓūmah.”

The manẓūmah encompasses the most prominent and essential issues of the science, providing a comprehensive overview while remaining concise and structured for teaching and memorization.

By presenting this framework, the poet effectively concludes the ten foundational principles of the science, with his final line beautifully capturing the ninth and tenth principles.

chapters.desc: The Imāmah is the succession to Prophethood in protecting the religion and managing worldly affairs in accordance with it. These five abyāt give its definition and its names, then the evidence from the Qurʾān, the Sunnah and the consensus of the Ummah that appointing an Imām is obligatory, since the religion cannot be established except through him.

verses.tr: The Imamate, the Prophet’s legacy in line, worldly governance with guardianship combine.

exp.en:
Its definition

Imāmah in Islam refers to the khilāfah an-nubuwwah, the continuation of the Prophet’s ﷺ mission, but in the context of leadership and administration after his passing. The phrase may be restated as:

“The Imāmah is the succession to Prophethood in protecting the religion and managing worldly affairs in accordance with it.”

The Imām is not a mere political figure but a guardian of faith and a leader of the believers who ensures that divine law governs public and private life.

Classical scholars have defined it in similar terms. Imām al-Māwardī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ said:

“The Imāmah is the succession to Prophethood in protecting the religion and governing the world by it.”

From this definition, we learn that:

  • The Imām (leader) is the successor of the Prophet ﷺ in his role of protecting the dīn (religion) and governing worldly matters.
  • His duty is to manage the interests of the Muslims, uphold justice, ensure the implementation of Sharīʿah, and safeguard the community’s affairs both spiritually and materially.

Thus, the Imāmah bridges the sacred and the practical, ensuring that worldly governance remains guided by divine law.

verses.tr: For (the protection of) religion, it is called the Khilāfah - an Imāmah and leadership over the believers.

exp.en:
The bayt opens with لِلدِّينِ, “of the religion”, which completes the definition given in the previous bayt: the Imāmah is the succession to Prophethood in guarding the religion and governing the world by it. It then turns to the names of this office.

Its names

This leadership role has been identified by various titles throughout Islamic tradition; however, the three primary names that are most associated with it are:

  1. الخِلَافَة (al-Khilāfah) – the Caliphate
  2. الإِمَامَة (al-Imāmah) – the Leadership
  3. إِمَارَةُ المُؤْمِنِينَ (Imārat al-Muʾminīn) – Commandership of the Believers

Each name carries its own origin and significance.

الإِمَامَة 1. Al-Imāmah

The title Imām appears in several aḥādīth, such as:

الأئمةُ من قُريشٍ …

“The leaders (الأئمة) are from Quraysh.” Aḥmad and al-Nasāʾī in al-Sunan al-Kubrā, from Anas ibn Mālik

This usage shows the legitimacy of the title “Imām” in reference to the political and religious leader of the Muslim community.

الخِلَافَة 2. Al-Khilāfah

The term Khalīfah (successor) is rooted in the Qurʾān itself, where Allah says:

﴿ثُمَّ جَعَلْنَاكُمْ خَلَائِفَ فِي الْأَرْضِ مِنْ بَعْدِهِمْ﴾

“Then We made you successors in the land after them.” Yūnus 10:14

Here, khulafāʾ (successors) denotes those who succeed others in authority and stewardship; hence, the ruler is called Khalīfah, as he succeeds the Prophet ﷺ in governing the Ummah according to divine guidance.

إِمَارَةُ المُؤْمِنِينَ 3. Amīr al-Muʾminīn

As for the title Amīr al-Muʾminīn, “Commander of the Believers”, it was first used for ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ.

It is narrated from al-Ḍaḥḥāk that when the Prophet ﷺ passed away, the people said to Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ:

“You are the Khalīfah of the Messenger of Allah.”

When Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ passed away, they said to ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ:

“You are the Khalīfah of the Khalīfah of the Messenger of Allah.”

So ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ said:

“That is too lengthy. When I die and someone succeeds me, will you say: the Khalīfah of the Khalīfah of the Khalīfah of the Messenger of Allah? You are the believers, and I am your commander, Amīr al-Muʾminīn.”

Thus, the first to be given the title Amīr al-Muʾminīn was ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, and from then on it became the recognized designation for the ruler of the Muslims.

Together, these titles reflect the spiritual, political, and administrative dimensions of Islamic leadership.

verses.tr: The verse “Appoint among you…” indicates its obligation; if you are three, then establish one (as leader).

exp.en:
The obligation of establishing the Imāmah

The obligation of appointing an Imām is established by the Qurʾān, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the Ummah.

Qurʾānic evidence

Allah commands, in the āyah the poet points to with its word يَأْمُرُكُمْ:

﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَأْمُرُكُمْ أَنْ تُؤَدُّوا الْأَمَانَاتِ إِلَىٰ أَهْلِهَا وَإِذَا حَكَمْتُمْ بَيْنَ النَّاسِ أَنْ تَحْكُمُوا بِالْعَدْلِ﴾

“Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to whom they are due and when you judge between people to judge with justice.” al-Nisāʾ 4:58

This āyah, as explained by al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, and other exegetes, serves as a proof for the obligation of appointing leaders: those who administer justice and safeguard the trust of governance among people.

Thus, the command to uphold justice necessarily implies the establishment of a governing authority.

Prophetic evidence

The Prophet ﷺ reinforced this principle through clear instructions. Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

إِذَا خَرَجَ ثَلَاثَةٌ فِي سَفَرٍ فَلْيُؤَمِّرُوْا أَحَدَهُمْ

“When three are on a journey, they must appoint one of them as leader.” Abū Dāwūd

He also said, in the narration of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ:

لَا يَحِلُّ لِثَلَاثَةِ نَفَرٍ يَكُوْنُوْنَ بِأَرْضِ فَلَاةٍ إِلَّا أَمَّرُوْا عَلَيْهِمْ أَحَدَهُمْ

“It is not permissible for three people to be in a desert without appointing one of them as their leader.” Aḥmad

Ibn Taymiyyah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ commented on this:

“If it has been made obligatory for the smallest of groups and the briefest of gatherings to appoint one among them, this serves as an indication (tanbīh) of the even greater obligation to do so in larger societies and enduring communities.”

In other words, if leadership is necessary for a group of three, it is even more essential for the Ummah at large, to ensure order, justice, and implementation of Sharīʿah.

verses.tr: And the one who dies without a pledge of allegiance, and likewise, the one who rebels against obedience (both are warned in hadith).

exp.en:
The warning against rebellion and neglecting allegiance

Rebellion and neglecting allegiance are serious matters in Islam, for they strike at the heart of unity and order within the Ummah. The Prophet ﷺ warned that severing ties with legitimate authority or living without bayʿah leads to chaos and a return to the ways of jāhiliyyah.

From ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

مَنْ خَلَعَ يَدًا مِّنْ طَاعَةٍ، لَقِيَ اللهَ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ لَا حُجَّةَ لَهُ، وَمَنْ مَاتَ وَلَيْسَ فِيْ عُنُقِهِ بَيْعَةٌ، مَاتَ مِيْتَةً جَاهِلِيَّةً

“Whoever withdraws his hand from obedience will meet Allah on the Day of Resurrection without a proof for himself; and whoever dies without a bayʿah around his neck dies a death of jāhiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance).” Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim

And in another narration, from Abū Hurayrah رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, the Prophet ﷺ said:

مَنْ خَرَجَ مِنَ الطَّاعَةِ، وَفَارَقَ الْجَمَاعَةَ فَمَاتَ، مَاتَ مِيْتَةً جَاهِلِيَّةً

“Whoever leaves obedience and separates from the community and dies, dies a death of jāhiliyyah.” Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim

These narrations illustrate that disobedience to legitimate authority and disunity within the community are not minor issues: they endanger the collective harmony of the Ummah and can result in a state akin to jāhiliyyah, where chaos and disunity prevail.

verses.ajuz: لِكَوۡنِ دِينٍ لَمۡ يُقَمۡ إِلَّا بِهِ
verses.tr: The scholars have agreed on the obligation of appointing him (the ruler), for the religion cannot be established except through him.

exp.en:
This wujūb (obligation) entails two distinct obligations:

  1. Upon those qualified for leadership: it is farḍ kifāyah (a collective obligation) that, among those who meet the conditions of Imāmah, one of them assumes this responsibility.
  2. Upon Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd (the electors): it is farḍ kifāyah upon those entrusted with authority, the scholars, jurists, and leaders of the community, to appoint an Imām whenever the position becomes vacant due to death, apostasy, or any other reason.

Consensus (ijmāʿ) on its obligation

This shows that leadership is not optional; it is the spine of the Ummah’s collective life. Without an Imām, neither can the laws of Islam be implemented nor its objectives fulfilled. Hence, scholars unanimously agreed, from the time of the Companions until today, on the necessity of appointing a leader for the Muslims, considering it a communal obligation (farḍ kifāyah).

This alludes to the universal principle in Uṣūl al-Fiqh:

“Whatever is necessary to fulfill an obligation becomes obligatory itself.”

Thus, since the upholding of the Dīn, the preservation of the Maqāṣid (higher objectives of Sharīʿah), and the protection of people’s interests cannot be achieved except through the existence of an Imām, the appointment of the Imām itself becomes an obligation.

chapters.desc: Leadership in Islam is not a privilege but an amānah (trust), and not everyone who desires it is worthy of it. Drawing on the Qurʾān, the Sunnah and the early practice of the Companions, the scholars set out ten conditions that must be present in the Imām, and the poet gathers all ten in two abyāt.

verses.tr: His conditions are Islam, maturity, and freedom, sound intellect, masculinity, and upright in character.

exp.en:
Since Khilāfah is one of the most vital pillars of governance in Islam, responsible for preserving the religion, establishing justice, and managing the affairs of the Ummah, it is only fitting that the Sharīʿah defines a clear set of conditions for the one who holds this immense trust.

Leadership in Islam is not a privilege but an amānah (trust), and thus, not everyone who desires it is worthy of it. The scholars, drawing from the Qurʾān, Sunnah, and early practice of the Companions, have outlined essential qualities that must be present in the Imām to ensure that his leadership fulfils its divine purpose.

The conditions are:

  1. Islam
  2. Maturity
  3. Freedom
  4. Sound intellect
  5. Maleness
  6. Uprightness
  7. Capability for ijtihād
  8. Kifāyah
  9. Qurashī lineage
  10. Physical soundness

These ten qualities form the framework through which the legitimacy and success of Islamic leadership are ensured.

1st Condition – Islam

The first and foremost condition is Islām itself.

The Khalīfah is the successor of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in preserving the dīn and governing the world through it. It is inconceivable that one who does not believe in Islam should lead the Muslim Ummah in protecting it.

Allah says:

﴿وَلَنْ يَجْعَلَ اللَّهُ لِلْكَافِرِينَ عَلَى الْمُؤْمِنِينَ سَبِيلًا﴾

“And Allah will never grant the disbelievers a way (of authority) over the believers.” al-Nisāʾ 4:141

This āyah establishes that a non-Muslim cannot have legal authority over Muslims.

The scholars have unanimously agreed on this condition. Imām al-Nawawī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ mentioned this consensus in his Sharḥ Muslim, and al-Ḥāfiẓ Ibn Ḥajar رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ affirmed it in Fatḥ al-Bārī.

Allah also says:

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أَطِيعُوا اللَّهَ وَأَطِيعُوا الرَّسُولَ وَأُولِي الْأَمْرِ مِنْكُمْ﴾

“O you who believe! Obey Allah, and obey the Messenger, and those in authority among you.” al-Nisāʾ 4:59

The phrase “among you” (minkum) clearly indicates that those in authority must be from among the believers themselves. The exegetes have explained ulū al-amr in two ways:

  • The rulers and leaders.
  • The scholars and people of knowledge.

Thus, the verse encompasses obedience to both: rulers who govern and scholars who guide, provided they are believers.

2nd Condition – Maturity (Bulūgh)

The Khalīfah must be of age and legally accountable (mukallaf). A child who has not reached maturity is exempted from religious obligation and requires a guardian. Such a person cannot be entrusted with the leadership of the entire Ummah.

As the Prophet ﷺ said:

رُفِعَ الْقَلَمُ عن ثلاثة: عن النائم حتى يَسْتَيْقِظَ، وعن الصبي حتى يَحْتَلِمَ، وعن المجنون حتى يَعْقِلَ

“The pen is lifted from three: the sleeping person until he wakes, the child until he reaches puberty, and the insane until he regains his senses.” Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasāʾī

Therefore, one who is not legally accountable cannot be entrusted with the collective responsibility of the Ummah.

3rd Condition – Freedom (Ḥurriyyah)

A slave cannot be appointed as Khalīfah, as he himself is under the ownership and authority of another. Leadership requires independence, and a slave does not possess authority even over himself. His will and decisions are subject to his master, so how could he possess authority over the entire Ummah?

The position of Imāmah requires complete independence in decision-making, which is inconsistent with slavery.

4th Condition – Sound Intellect (ʿAql)

Sanity and sound judgment are indispensable. Madness or insanity negates legal accountability (taklīf). The responsibilities of the Imāmah require sound intellect and rational judgment in managing public affairs. The insane person cannot manage his own wealth or decisions and therefore cannot manage the affairs of a nation.

5th Condition – Being Male (Dhukūrah)

This condition is agreed upon by the scholars. It is not permissible for a woman to hold the position of Khalīfah or Sulṭān.

The Prophet ﷺ said:

لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ وَلَّوْا أَمْرَهُمُ امْرَأَةً

“A people who entrust their affairs to a woman will never prosper.” Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī

This ḥadīth is clear textual evidence indicating that the role of Imāmah Kubrā (the supreme leadership) is restricted to men. The role requires public leadership, attending councils, leading armies, and direct involvement in societal and political affairs, all of which are obligations that, according to the Sharīʿah, are designated for men.

6th Condition – Uprightness (ʿAdālah)

The Khalīfah must be just and upright.

Imām al-Māwardī described the just ruler as:

“That one be truthful in speech, apparent in trustworthiness, chaste from the unlawful, distant from sins, free from deceit, and governed by moral conduct in both religion and worldly dealings.”

The evidence is in Allah’s statement to Ibrāhīm عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ:

﴿قَالَ إِنِّي جَاعِلُكَ لِلنَّاسِ إِمَامًا ۖ قَالَ وَمِنْ ذُرِّيَّتِي ۖ قَالَ لَا يَنَالُ عَهْدِي الظَّالِمِينَ﴾

“Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people.” [Ibrāhīm said:] “And of my descendants?” [Allah] said: “My covenant does not extend to the wrongdoers.” al-Baqarah 2:124

This verse establishes that leadership is a divine ʿahd (trust) that cannot be given to the unjust or corrupt.

verses.tr: Also required are ijtihād (scholarly insight) and sound judgment and courage, Quraysh lineage, and being free from physical defects.

exp.en:
7th Condition – Capability for Ijtihād (scholarly qualification)

The Imām should possess the knowledge and capacity to perform ijtihād, which refers to a level of knowledge sufficient to issue legal verdicts (fatāwā), enabling him to judge between people and lead with insight into Sharīʿah rulings.

Imām al-Juwaynī said in Ghiyāth al-Umam:

“It is a condition that the Imām be a mujtahid, attaining the level of those qualified to give legal verdicts, and no disagreement has been transmitted regarding this requirement.”

In times of necessity, when no mujtahid is available, Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd can appoint a knowledgeable and capable leader who is not a mujtahid, on the condition that he consults scholars and refrains from acting independently in sharʿī rulings.

8th Condition – Competence and Capability (Kifāyah)

Kifāyah encompasses both strategic intelligence and courage.

  • Strategic insight: the Imām must be capable of wise decision-making, public administration, and managing the interests of the Ummah.
  • Courage: to defend the Ummah, protect its borders, and enforce justice with firmness and authority.

Imām al-Juwaynī said:

توقُّد الرَّأي في عظائم الأمور، والنظر في مغبات العواقب، وهذه الصفة ينتجها العقل، ويهذبها التدرّب في طريق التجارب

“He must be sharp in judgment regarding great affairs, insightful of outcomes. This quality is born of intellect and refined through experience.”

Thus, leadership requires not only intelligence but tested wisdom and the strength to act decisively when needed.

9th Condition – Qurashī Lineage (Qurashiyyah)

The ninth condition for Imāmah is that the Imām must be from the tribe of Quraysh. This condition is established through multiple authentic narrations. Muʿāwiyah رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say:

إنَّ هَذَا الأمر في قريشٍ، لا يعاديهم أحد إلا كَبَّهُ اللهُ في النّارِ عَلى وَجْهِهِ، مَا أَقامُوْا الدِّيْنَ

“This matter (of leadership) will remain among Quraysh. No one will oppose them without Allah throwing him on his face into the Fire, so long as they uphold the religion.” al-Bukhārī

He ﷺ also said:

لَا يَزَالُ هَذَا الْأَمْرُ فِي قُرَيْشٍ مَا بَقِيَ مِنْهُمُ اثْنَانِ

“This affair will remain among Quraysh as long as two of them remain.” al-Bukhārī

Imām al-Nawawī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ explains:

“These aḥādīth and their likes are clear evidence that the Khilāfah is restricted to Quraysh. Consensus was established upon this during the era of the Companions and remains binding thereafter. Whoever differs from it is refuted by this ijmāʿ.”

Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ likewise stated:

“The requirement of Qurashiyyah is the unanimous view of all scholars. Abū Bakr and ʿUmar used it as a proof against the Anṣār on the day of Saqīfah, and no one objected; thus it became a matter of consensus.”

However, scholars also acknowledged exceptions in situations of necessity. If the people of authority (Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd) cannot find a qualified Qurashī candidate and the unity of Muslims would be at risk, the appointment of a non-Qurashī may be accepted to prevent greater harm.

As for the wisdom behind this condition, the scholars explained that it was not about racial privilege but social cohesion. The scholars state that the Prophet ﷺ restricted the Imāmah to Quraysh due to the potential for dispute over leadership. Quraysh was a large and respected tribe, traditionally obeyed by the Arabs, and would always have among them men of competence. This restriction, therefore, prevented intertribal conflict and preserved unity. Yet, when choice and capacity exist, the condition stands.

10th Condition – Physical Soundness (Salāmah)

The Khalīfah should be free from physical impairments that prevent him from fulfilling his duties.

There is no disagreement on the requirement of sight, for instance. Imām al-Māwardī states:

“Loss of sight prevents both the appointment and continuation of the Imāmah. If blindness occurs after appointment, it invalidates the Imāmah, because blindness disqualifies one from being a judge or witness — thus more so from being an Imām.”

Similarly, hearing and speech are essential, for without them, the communication of commands, reception of counsel, and administration of justice would be impaired.

If these defects arise after the appointment, scholars have differed:

  • Some hold that he must be removed, as these prevent him from fulfilling his duties.
  • Others allow him to remain, provided he can continue to govern effectively through delegation.

Thus, these ten conditions collectively preserve the integrity, justice, and functionality of Islamic leadership, ensuring that the one entrusted with the Ummah’s affairs is religiously upright, legally accountable, intellectually capable, physically sound, strategically competent, and socially accepted within the framework laid down by the Prophet ﷺ and affirmed by the consensus of the Ummah.

chapters.desc: Because the office of the Khalīfah is one of immense responsibility, the Sharīʿah outlines specific duties to ensure the welfare of the Ummah and the proper administration of its affairs. The poet first gives the ten primary duties enumerated by jurists such as al-Māwardī, then their branches: the rulings on non-Muslim residents, working with public interests, and conduct with other nations in war, peace and treaties.

verses.tr: It is binding upon the ruler to safeguard the religion, and to protect the frontiers through fortification.

exp.en:
Because the office of the Khalīfah is one of immense responsibility, the Sharīʿah outlines specific primary duties to ensure the welfare of the Ummah and the proper administration of its affairs. Classical jurists such as al-Māwardī, Abū Yaʿlā, and al-Juwaynī رَحِمَهُمُ اللَّهُ have enumerated these duties, identifying ten fundamental responsibilities that every Khalīfah must observe:

  1. Ḥifẓ ad-Dīn — safeguarding the religion
  2. Taḥṣīn al-Thughūr — fortifying the frontiers (defence)
  3. Iqāmat al-Ḥudūd — establishing and enforcing the legal limits (ḥudūd)
  4. Al-Qaḍāʾ — appointing and enforcing the judiciary
  5. Jibāyah al-Fayʾ — collecting public revenues (bayt al-māl)
  6. Taqdīr al-ʿAṭāʾ — determining and distributing stipends and charitable allocations
  7. Mubāsharah — direct supervision and personal oversight of affairs
  8. Tamnīn al-Subul — securing the roads and public ways (safety of travel and commerce)
  9. Jihād — conducting and organising legitimate military action when required
  10. Ikhtiyār khayr ʿāmil — appointing competent officials and supervisors

These ten duties serve as the framework for the Khalīfah’s governance. They provide a clear guideline for maintaining religion, justice, security, public welfare, and the proper functioning of the state. This bayt names the first two of them.

1. Ḥifẓ ad-Dīn — safeguarding the religion (the first and foremost duty)

This is the first and most foundational obligation of the Khalīfah. As Imām al-Māwardī explains:

“Ḥifẓ ad-dīn consists in keeping the religion on its sound foundations as understood by the predecessors: clarifying truth to those led astray by doubts, enforcing rights and limits required by the Sharīʿah, preventing corruption and protecting the community from deviation.”

Ibn Ḥazm and Ibn Taymiyyah echo this central purpose: the offices of rule exist primarily to preserve the religion and those worldly means without which religion cannot be preserved.

Two practical branches of ḥifẓ ad-dīn are as follows:

  • Preserving the outward rites and public religious order (e.g. ensuring the call to prayer, congregational prayer, and the collection and distribution of zakāh). If a community openly abandons a sharʿī obligation, the ruler calls them to reform and, if they persist, resists them (e.g. the consensus on combating those who withheld zakāh in the time of Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ).
  • Guarding against apparent evil and disbelief: curbing public immorality, silencing false innovations, commissioning teachers and scholars, and rebutting the arguments of sectarians so the creed and practice of the community remain intact.

2. Taḥṣīn al-Thughūr — fortification and defence of the frontiers

The thughūr are border regions and coastal defences.

The khalīfah must protect the borders, land and sea, where enemies can penetrate. Guarding the thughūr means stationing garrisons, building forts and watch-posts, keeping night-and-day surveillance, and sustaining readiness so that the Muslim lands are not exposed to surprise attack. Coastal cities, islands and border provinces are included; the aim is constant preparedness and deterrence.

verses.tr: To implement the prescribed punishments along with the judicial system, to collect the spoils and distribute stipends.

exp.en:
3. Iqāmat al-Ḥudūd — establishing the ḥudūd (legal penalties)

Al-Māwardī puts the enforcement of ḥudūd among the ruler’s essential tasks:

“Establishing the ḥudūd to protect the sanctities set by Allah, prevent public harm, and secure the rights of people from corruption and destruction.”

The Khalīfah is responsible for ensuring that legal limits are applied with justice and that punishments are executed when the required standards of proof and process are met.

4. Al-Qaḍāʾ — the judiciary: appointment and enforcement of the qāḍī

This means appointing competent judges to settle disputes according to Sharīʿah, enforcing court rulings, and maintaining judicial independence.

The ruler sees to the dignity and effectiveness of the courts: judgments must carry weight, execution must be effected, and recalcitrant parties must be compelled to comply.

The Prophet ﷺ sent Muʿādh ibn Jabal رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ to Yemen as a qāḍī, and the Khulafāʾ followed this tradition by appointing judges for each region.

5. Jibāyah al-Fayʾ — collection of public revenue (bayt al-māl)

“Fayʾ” broadly denotes the lawful public resources appointed to the treasury. It includes:

  1. Treaty funds: funds obtained through treaty, without fighting.
  2. War booty: part of the spoils and shares of the war booty (ghanīmah).
  3. Kharāj: land tax collected from agricultural land.
  4. Jizyah: tax levied on non-Muslims in Islamic states.
  5. Zakāh: mandatory charity for Muslims, a percentage of wealth.
  6. Unclaimed wealth: wealth that has no known owner.

The ruler must ensure proper collection and fair distribution, so the state has resources for defence, administration, and public welfare.

6. Taqdīr al-ʿAṭāʾ — determining and distributing allowances and stipends

The sixth duty of the Khalīfah is Taqdīr al-ʿAṭāʾ, which refers to the fair and prudent management of the state’s financial resources, both income and expenditure.

Imām al-Māwardī defines it as:

“Determining the stipends and what is deserved in the Bayt al-Māl without extravagance or negligence, and ensuring payment at its due time, neither in advance nor delay.”

In essence, this duty encompasses overseeing the public treasury (Bayt al-Māl), setting financial priorities, and ensuring that distribution is governed by justice, transparency, and the welfare of the Ummah. It demands not only financial competence but also moral discernment and political foresight.

Historically, this duty was exemplified by the Rightly Guided Caliphs. Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ would divide the surplus of the Bayt al-Māl annually, distributing it equally among the Muslims after state expenses were met. His approach reflected the ideal of equality and simplicity in the early Muslim community.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, however, introduced a more structured system of distribution. Recognising differences in service and contribution to Islam, he established a tiered allocation system. The Ahl al-Badr (participants of Badr) were granted higher stipends than others, followed by those who pledged at al-Riḍwān, those who accepted Islam before the Conquest of Makkah, and finally those who came after. The Mothers of the Believers and the Ahl al-Bayt were given special stipends in recognition of their status and service.

This system reflected ʿUmar’s رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ administrative foresight and his understanding that justice is not always uniformity but giving each their due according to merit and need.

verses.tr: He directly oversees the people’s affairs, secures the roads, strives in jihad, and appoints the best in every affair.

exp.en:
7. Mubāsharah — personal oversight and direct supervision

The seventh duty of the Khalīfah is Mubāsharah, meaning his personal supervision and active engagement in the affairs of governance. This duty ensures that leadership does not become distant, ceremonial, or dependent solely on intermediaries.

Imām al-Māwardī defines this responsibility with remarkable precision, saying:

“He must personally oversee the affairs and examine the conditions of the people, so that he may be attentive to the administration of the Ummah and the protection of the religion. He should not rely entirely on delegation, becoming distracted by pleasure or even by worship, for the entrusted may betray and the advisor may deceive.”

This statement highlights a delicate balance: while the Khalīfah may delegate tasks, he must never detach from direct governance. His vigilance ensures that justice is upheld, corruption is curbed, and no segment of society is neglected. The example of ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ personally receiving complaints, investigating governors, and acting on reports illustrates the required hands-on leadership.

Thus, Mubāsharah requires that the leader remain informed of both public matters and the conditions of his subjects, visiting regions, listening to grievances, and supervising officials. A leader who governs from a distance risks being misled or exploited by those beneath him.

8. Tamnīn al-Subul — securing roads and public ways (safety of travel and commerce)

The Khalīfah must ensure safe passage for people and goods: combat highwaymen and criminals, and apply ḥadd al-ḥirābah when necessary, ensuring people’s safety.

Secured roads increase public welfare and economic stability; protecting routes is thus part of governance and public order.

9. Jihād — military action when necessary to protect religion and society

Jihād in this context is the ruler’s responsibility to fight those who oppose Islam after being invited to it, either until they embrace Islam or live peacefully under Muslim rule (dhimmah).

Al-Māwardī and later jurists articulate that jihād is entrusted to the Imām: he organises, sustains, and conducts campaigns when required, ensuring that warfare is directed by sharʿī goals and discipline, following the ḥadīth of the Prophet ﷺ:

أُمِرْتُ أَنْ أُقَاتِلَ النَّاسَ حَتَّى يَقُوْلُوْا لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللهُ …

“I was commanded to fight people until they say ‘lā ilāha illā Allāh’…”

10. Ikhtiyār khayr ʿāmil — appointing competent officials (selection of the best agents)

The tenth duty of the Khalīfah is to carefully select the best individuals for public office, those who combine competence with integrity. The strength of a state is not only in its laws and policies but in the people entrusted to implement them.

A just leader, therefore, must ensure that every responsibility is given to one who is both capable and sincere.

Imām al-Māwardī beautifully summarizes this obligation:

“It is to appoint those who are trustworthy, and to entrust the sincere in what he delegates to them of tasks and what he assigns to them of wealth — so that the affairs remain regulated and the public funds safeguarded.”

This principle ensures that authority is exercised through trustworthy deputies and advisors who act as extensions of the leader’s justice, not as substitutes for it. Neglect in appointments can lead to oppression, mismanagement, and loss of public trust, all of which weaken the very foundation of governance.

Thus, together, these ten duties uphold religion, safeguard society, ensure justice, support public finances, and maintain order. The poet summarizes them in three abyāt, of which this is the last.

verses.tr: Among the duties placed on the Imāms, is enforcing laws for the Ahl al-Dhimma (non-Muslim citizens under Muslim lands).

exp.en:
Secondary duties (branches of the primary duties)

Because the primary duties of the Khalīfah are vast and interlinked, several crucial tasks fall beneath them as distinct sub-branches. These secondary duties deserve focused attention because they involve specialised rulings, political judgment, and long-term administration. They may be grouped into three major clusters:

  1. Applying the rulings related to non-Muslim residents: aḥkām ahl al-dhimmah, and related categories. This governs how the state protects and manages the affairs of non-Muslims living within its borders, ensuring justice, protection, and fulfilment of rights and obligations.
  2. Managing public interests (al-maṣāliḥ): distinguishing between sanctioned, rejected, and discretionary interests, and acting accordingly. This concerns how the Khalīfah governs matters of policy, administration, and welfare in areas not explicitly defined by revelation, ensuring that all measures align with Sharīʿah objectives and serve the common good.
  3. Diplomatic relations and conduct with other nations: peace, war, and treaties. This includes conducting diplomacy, establishing truces or alliances, waging legitimate warfare when required, and managing all external dealings in a way that preserves the dignity, safety, and interests of the Muslim Ummah.

These three areas together reflect the Khalīfah’s ongoing responsibility to safeguard both the internal and external order of the Ummah, in belief, governance, and security.

The rulings related to non-Muslim residents

This area, the first of the three and the subject of this bayt, falls under several primary duties at once, mainly ḥifẓ ad-dīn, jibāyah al-fayʾ, and jihād, yet it is usually treated as a separate field of policy because of its technical breadth.

Jurists wrote whole books on the subject; its practical rules are core to the state.

verses.tr: Those granted safety, allies, or foes in fight - each has a ruling that must be applied right.

exp.en:
The four categories of non-Muslims and the ruling for each

Non-Muslims who enter or live in Muslim lands are classified into four types. Each category carries its own ruling:

  • Mustaʾmin: granted safe-conduct for a temporary stay.
  • Muʿāhid: treaty partner with mutual obligations.
  • Muḥārib: hostile combatant.
  • Ahl al-Dhimmah: permanent residents under covenant.

مُسْتَأْمِنٌ 1. Mustaʾmin (the one granted safe-conduct)

Definition: one who enters Muslim territory under amān, a specific guarantee of safety.

Example: historically by treaty, now commonly by visa or permit for tourism, business, work, family visits, etc.

Ruling: he is secure in person and property for the duration of his stay; no aggression is permitted against him or his possessions. Even if he is a subject of a country hostile to Muslims, his personal security and rights are preserved while under Muslim protection.

Once their period of stay or amān expires, they must leave peacefully or renew the permission.

This category includes envoys and ambassadors.

مُعَاهِدٌ 2. Muʿāhid (the treaty partner)

Definition: subjects of a state that has a treaty with the Muslims (a state covenant).

Example: the Treaty of Ḥudaybiyyah is the classical model, which the Prophet ﷺ made with Quraysh; both sides agreed not to fight for a fixed period.

Ruling: they are protected; Muslims do not fight them and may not attack their lands so long as the treaty stands. However, if the other side violates the agreement, the Muslims may respond appropriately.

Allah says:

﴿فَأَتِمُّوا إِلَيْهِمْ عَهْدَهُمْ إِلَىٰ مُدَّتِهِمْ ۚ إِنَّ اللَّهَ يُحِبُّ الْمُتَّقِينَ﴾

“So fulfill their treaty until their term ends. Indeed, Allah loves the righteous.” al-Tawbah 9:4

And the Prophet ﷺ said:

مَن قَتَلَ نَفْسًا مُعاهَدًا لَمْ يَرِحْ رائِحَةَ الجَنَّةِ

“Whoever kills a person under covenant will not smell the fragrance of Paradise.” al-Bukhārī

مُحَارِبٌ 3. Muḥārib (the hostile combatant)

Definition: a person belonging to a nation or group that is at war with Muslims, with no treaty or amān between them, or one who enters Muslim lands as an enemy.

Ruling: he is treated as an enemy combatant; war rulings apply.

Thus, fighting them is permissible when war is declared and justified. Even then, the Sharīʿah sets strict rules:

  • No killing of women, children, monks, or non-combatants.
  • No mutilation or betrayal.
  • War is only permitted under a legitimate Imām and for just causes, never for aggression.

أَهْلُ الذِّمَّةِ 4. Ahl al-Dhimmah (permanent non-Muslim residents under covenant)

Definition: non-Muslim residents who live permanently in the Muslim state under a covenant of protection (ʿaqd al-dhimmah).

Ruling: their lives and property are inviolable; in return they pay jizyah (a tax).

Classical practice exempted women and the poor from jizyah; the wealthy paid a fixed annual contribution (historically small sums, e.g. one dīnār annually from the wealthy).

Ahl al-dhimmah enjoy civic protection and specific legal statuses.

verses.tr: He should act upon maṣāliḥ mursalah (unrestricted public interests) with reason and sight, preferring the stronger view, setting aside the slight.

exp.en:
Working with public interests (al-maṣāliḥ)

All duties of the Khalīfah are carried out through means, and those means must be assessed against sharʿī criteria. Al-Māwardī and later jurists classify interests into three types; the Khalīfah must act differently in each case.

1. Maṣāliḥ muʿtabarah — interests recognised by the Sharīʿah

Definition: these are ends the Sharīʿah explicitly seeks: preservation of religion, life, intellect, lineage and property (the five ḍarūriyyāt).

Examples: prohibiting wine to protect reason; prescribing ḥudūd to protect property and honour.

When an action is in this category, the ruler works to secure it.

2. Maṣāliḥ mulghā — disregarded interests

Definition: these are interests rejected by the Sharīʿah because the harm outweighs the benefit.

Example: trading in intoxicants or gambling. Although these activities might economically benefit a state, their social harms render them unacceptable, as stated in the Qurʾān:

﴿يَسْأَلُونَكَ عَنِ الْخَمْرِ وَالْمَيْسِرِ ۖ قُلْ فِيهِمَا إِثْمٌ كَبِيرٌ وَمَنَافِعُ لِلنَّاسِ وَإِثْمُهُمَا أَكْبَرُ مِنْ نَفْعِهِمَا﴾

“They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and some benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit.” al-Baqarah 2:219

3. Maṣāliḥ mursalah — discretionary or unstated interests: matters the Sharīʿah is silent about

Definition: these are interests about which the Sharīʿah has remained silent, neither affirming nor nullifying them, but which serve the higher objectives of Islam without contradicting its principles.

Examples: the Caliphs made decisions guided by such interests. Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ compiled the Qurʾān into a single muṣḥaf to safeguard the religion, while ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ introduced the Hijrī calendar, organised state records (dawāwīn), and established prison systems: all measures based on maṣāliḥ mursalah intended to benefit the Ummah.

In contemporary contexts, these principles are reflected in practices such as the implementation of traffic regulations, speed limits, and signals.

The ruler may enact such measures when they serve public welfare and do not contravene the Sharīʿah.

Balancing interests and harms — a working rule

  • When two interests conflict, the ruler must weigh and prioritise: preserve the greater interest even if a lesser one is postponed.
  • When two harms conflict, avert the greater harm even if that requires tolerating a lesser harm.

This is the standard practical rule in maqāṣid reasoning.

Examples. Allah says:

﴿وَلَا تَسُبُّوا الَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ فَيَسُبُّوا اللَّهَ عَدْوًا بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ﴾

“And do not insult those they invoke besides Allah, lest they insult Allah in enmity without knowledge.” al-Anʿām 6:108

Mocking idols is a benefit, but it leads to a greater harm, that they would insult Allah, so it was forbidden.

The Prophet ﷺ refrained from demolishing the Kaʿbah and rebuilding it to Ibrāhīm’s عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ plan immediately (though it was beneficial) because the people’s state of faith could not bear the shock; a greater harm would result. As he said to ʿĀʾishah رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا:

“O ʿĀʾishah, were it not that your people have only recently left disbelief, I would have demolished the Kaʿbah and rebuilt it upon the foundations of Ibrāhīm عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ, giving it two doors, one to the east and one to the west.” al-Bukhārī

The same applies to the Prophet ﷺ not killing the hypocrites in Madinah, though doing so might protect the community. He avoided it because it would lead to greater harm: outsiders would think he kills his own companions, turning people away from Islam.

This shows caution in pursuing reforms even where benefit exists.

Thus, the Khalīfah should seek to implement sharʿī rules fully but may be constrained by realities (political, military, social). Where full enforcement would cause greater harm or cannot be achieved, he works prudently, applying what he can and postponing what he cannot, always aiming to maximise overall benefit.

This explains why rulers historically sometimes delayed or staged reforms rather than imposing radical overnight change: practical wisdom, not weakness.

verses.tr: With nations, he deals in honor and peace, in war, in treaties, respect must not cease.

exp.en:
Diplomatic relations and conduct with other nations

Among the duties of the rulers is understanding Fiqh al-ʿAlāqāt ad-Duwaliyyah, the jurisprudence of international relations. This includes knowing how the Muslim state should deal with other nations, whether in times of war, peace, or when treaties exist between them.

This branch of knowledge is often referred to as “as-Siyar” (the laws of war and peace in Islam). Scholars such as Imām al-Awzāʿī, Imām Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan ash-Shaybānī, and Imām Abū Yūsuf رَحِمَهُمُ اللَّهُ wrote important works on this subject.

Thus, these responsibilities outline a system of leadership that is as comprehensive as it is principled. Every duty, from safeguarding faith to managing foreign relations, works toward preserving the unity, justice, and moral strength of the Ummah.

What scholars like al-Māwardī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and others detailed across pages, the poet captures in just a few lines, condensing the essence of Islamic governance into a handful of abyāt.

chapters.desc: Just as the Imām bears great responsibilities toward the Ummah, the Ummah in turn owes him certain rights: obedience, sincere counsel, protection, honour and support. These rights preserve harmony between the ruler and the ruled, ensuring that leadership remains a source of unity, not conflict.

verses.tr: His due is obedience, advice that’s sincere, protection, respect, and support, that’s clear.

exp.en:
Just as the Imām bears great responsibilities toward the Ummah, the Ummah in turn owes him certain rights. These rights preserve harmony between the ruler and the ruled, ensuring that leadership remains a source of unity, not conflict. The key rights of the Imām are:

  1. Obedience
  2. Sincere counsel
  3. Protection
  4. Honour
  5. Support

الطَّاعَةُ 1. Obedience

Allah commands the believers:

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أَطِيعُوا اللَّهَ وَأَطِيعُوا الرَّسُولَ وَأُولِي الْأَمْرِ مِنْكُمْ﴾

“O you who believe, obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and those in authority among you.” al-Nisāʾ 4:59

The obedience due to rulers is not absolute but conditional: it follows obedience to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. The Qurʾān’s omission of the second verb “obey” before “those in authority” signifies that their obedience is dependent, not independent.

The Prophet ﷺ said, in the narration of Ibn ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا:

عَلى المَرْءِ المُسْلِم السَّمْعُ والطَّاعَةُ فِيما أَحَبَّ وكَرِهَ، إِلَّا أَنْ يُؤْمَرَ بِمَعْصِيَةٍ، فَإِذا أُمِرَ بِمَعْصِيَةٍ فَلا سَمْعَ وَلا طاعَةَ

“A Muslim must listen and obey in what he likes and dislikes, unless commanded to disobey Allah. If he is commanded to disobey Allah, there is no listening and no obedience.” al-Bukhārī and Muslim

Hence, obedience is due in what is lawful and just, but never in sin or oppression.

النَّصِيحَةُ 2. Sincere counsel

Tamīm ad-Dārī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ reported that the Prophet ﷺ said:

الدِّينُ النَّصِيحَةُ. قُلْنا: لِمَنْ؟ قالَ: لِلَّهِ ولِكِتابِهِ، ولِرَسولِهِ، ولأَئِمَّةِ المُسْلِمِينَ، وعامَّتِهِمْ

“Religion is sincere counsel.” We said, “To whom?” He said: “To Allah, His Book, His Messenger, the leaders of the Muslims, and their common folk.” Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim

Sincere advice to rulers means assisting them in righteousness, reminding them gently when they err, and maintaining loyalty and honesty in one’s dealings. It is not flattery or aiding them in wrongdoing.

الْحِمَايَةُ 3. Protection

Protecting the Imām from harm is part of safeguarding the stability of the Ummah, but this duty is bound by justice.

Imām Mālik said:

“If the ruler is like ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, it is obligatory upon the people to defend him and fight alongside him. But if he is otherwise, then leave him to what he deserves; Allah will take retribution from the oppressor through another oppressor, and then from both.”

Thus, protection is not blind allegiance but a defence of rightful authority for the sake of order and justice.

تَوْقِيرُهُ وَنُصْرَتُهُ 4. Honour and support

Honouring a just ruler is part of showing reverence to Allah.

Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ reported that the Prophet ﷺ said:

إِنَّ مِنْ إِجْلالِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى: إِكْرَامَ ذِي الشَّيْبَةِ المُسْلِمِ، وَحَامِلِ الْقُرآنِ غَيْرِ الْغَالِي فِيهِ والجَافِي عَنْهُ، وإِكْرَامَ ذِي السُّلْطَانِ المُقْسِطِ

“Part of honouring Allah is to show respect to a grey-haired Muslim, the carrier of the Qurʾān who neither exaggerates nor neglects it, and the just ruler.” Abū Dāwūd

Honour entails speaking to him with dignity, avoiding public humiliation, and supporting him in implementing justice. It is through such mutual respect that authority retains its moral weight and legitimacy.

These rights form the ethical bond between ruler and ruled. They balance accountability with respect, and authority with compassion.

chapters.en: The Ways of Appointing the Imām
chapters.desc: This chapter discusses the ways by which a Khalīfah, Imām, Sultan or Amīr al-Muʾminīn may come to authority: selection by Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd, designation or bequest, and overpowering or forceful seizure. It then turns to the natural question that follows: who has the authority to choose him, and what qualities must they have?

verses.tr: He is appointed through the choice of ahl al-ʿaqd, the wise and true. Or by the covenant left for him to pursue.

exp.en:
This chapter discusses the ways by which a Khalīfah, Imām, Sultan, or Amīr al-Muʾminīn may come to authority. There are three main ways by which the position of imāmah or leadership may be assumed:

  1. اخْتِيَارُ أَهْلِ الْحَلِّ وَالْعَقْدِ: selection by those who are qualified to appoint and remove the ruler (Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd).
  2. الْوَصِيَّةُ وَالِاسْتِخْلَافُ: by designation or bequest.
  3. الْقَهْرُ وَالِاسْتِيلَاءُ (التَّغَلُّبُ): by overpowering or forceful seizure.

Below we explain each method, its meaning, its validity, and the scholarly positions and practical limits associated with it.

1. By selection of Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd

This is the primary and preferred method. When the community faces succession, those qualified to appoint, the Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd, gather and choose a person to take charge.

أَهْلُ الْحَلِّ وَالْعَقْدِ Who are they?

Literally, al-ḥall is removal (dismissing the ruler) and al-ʿaqd is appointment (binding the office).

Thus, Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd are those who possess legitimate authority to appoint or depose the ruler. They are the scholars, leaders, and influential figures whose agreement ensures unity and strength among the Muslims.

Example: This was the method used by the Companions after the Prophet ﷺ passed away. They gathered, consulted one another, and after discussion and differing opinions, unanimously chose Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ as the first caliph of Islam.

Legal effect: This approach is considered the preferred standard; the Imām gains legitimate authority when appointed by those responsible.

2. By designation or bequest

This refers to when an existing ruler appoints his successor before his death.

Examples: This was done by Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, who, sensing his approaching death, appointed ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ as the next caliph. The Companions unanimously accepted this appointment.

Similarly, when ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ neared death, he did not name a single successor but rather appointed a council of six Companions to choose among themselves, a form of shūrā (consultation) that also falls under this method.

verses.tr: He is appointed also through dominance and lawful command - but beware of bloodshed across the land.

exp.en:
3. By overpowering or forceful seizure

This is the most controversial method, also known as al-taghallub: when a person seizes power by force and establishes control.

Its types:

  1. After the previous Imām’s death, before the appointment of a successor.
  2. While a just Imām is in place (rebellion against a legitimate ruler).
  3. Taking over from an unqualified ruler.

Scholarly positions and considerations

Validity when conditions are met: If the conqueror possesses the conditions of Imāmah (Islam, competence, etc.) and, by force, unites the community, many jurists count his accession as established, and his bayʿah becomes effective, to avoid prolonged fitnah and bloodshed. Al-Nawawī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ explains that:

“When someone who gathers the qualifications seizes authority to restore order, his rule may be regarded as valid for the sake of unity.”

If conditions are lacking: If the conqueror is manifestly unqualified (fāsiq, ignorant), jurists differ. The Shāfiʿī school has two views: some hold that his accession is established to prevent division; others deny its validity.

Why tolerate a conqueror?

While this method is not praiseworthy, if the ruler who takes power by force succeeds in maintaining stability, implementing the Sharīʿah, protecting the Ummah, and preventing chaos, he is recognized as the ruler to avoid greater bloodshed.

This principle is derived from the maxim:

“Preventing a greater harm takes precedence over pursuing a lesser good.”

Example: ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān seized power during the Umayyad period. Though his rise involved injustice and conflict, once he established authority, the scholars and leaders accepted his rule, because through him the frontiers of Islam were defended, laws were applied, and the interests of the Ummah were maintained.

Thus, their acceptance was not approval of his initial wrongdoing, but a choice to preserve unity and prevent greater harm.

verses.tr: (Ahl al-Ḥall wal-ʿAqd) Those of authority are men of worth, the scholars, leaders, and people well-known on earth.

exp.en:
After understanding how the Khalīfah is appointed, a natural question follows: who has the authority to choose him? Islam does not leave this decision open to just anyone; it entrusts it to a specific group known as Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd.

Who they are

Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd are those who have the right to “tie and untie”: to appoint and to remove a ruler. In other words, they are the representatives of the Ummah in such major decisions.

The scholars describe them as the learned, the leaders, and the respected figures among the people. Imām al-Nawawī said:

“They are the scholars, the chiefs, and the influential people whose agreement unites the community.”

So, they include senior scholars, commanders, tribal heads, and people of position and wisdom whose word carries weight in society. When they agree on an Imām, the rest of the Ummah follows, and unity is achieved through their consensus.

It is also important to understand that defining who exactly counts as Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd, and how they are chosen, is a matter of public interest (maṣāliḥ mursalah) and political organization (siyāsah sharʿiyyah). That means Muslim communities may organize this differently, through councils, organizing systems, procedures, and consultation committees, as long as it serves the same goal: ensuring that leadership is legitimate and rooted in Sharīʿah principles.
