Example: The Prophet ﷺ did not appoint a successor. Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ exercised ijtihād by ensuring the community chose a successor, seeing it as in the public interest. ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ structured the process by having six Companions choose among themselves, thereby reflecting public interest.

In modern contexts, countries may establish councils or designate a specific number of individuals for this purpose, which is a continuation of the principle of maṣāliḥ mursalah.

verses.tr: Their conditions: integrity paired with insight, and knowledge of the ranks of leaders in sight.

exp.en:
Their conditions

The scholars mention three key qualities that must be found in those who hold this responsibility:

عَدَالَةٌ Integrity, justice (ʿadālah)

They must be upright, honest, and known for integrity. How could corrupt people choose a just ruler? The one who gives bayʿah must himself be worthy of it. Justice is required for witnesses, judges, and rulers, so it is even more fitting for those who choose the ruler.

حِكْمَةٌ Wisdom (ḥikmah)

They must have the ability to judge situations fairly, to weigh benefits and harms, and to understand what will best serve the Ummah. Wisdom helps them make balanced decisions. For example, sometimes the fully qualified Imām is not available. In such cases:

  • If the community is strong and the threat is internal (ignorance, innovation), a learned Imām is preferred, with military leaders supporting him.
  • If the community is weak and external threats are present, a strong, courageous leader may be chosen, even if less learned, with scholars as advisors to compensate for his lack of knowledge.
  • If the successor is a child, guardians are appointed to manage affairs until the child comes of age.

عِلْمُهُمْ مَرَاتِبَ الْأَئِمَّةِ Knowledge of leadership (ʿilm bi-marātib al-aʾimmah)

This does not mean they must be great scholars in every field, but they must know the ranks and abilities of potential leaders: who among them is more capable, more knowledgeable, more courageous, and more likely to unite the Ummah.

So, these are the people who carry the heavy responsibility of selecting a ruler: the just, the wise, and the knowledgeable. They act not for personal gain but for the stability and guidance of the Ummah.

chapters.desc: Once Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd have identified the most suitable candidate for Imāmah, his leadership is formalized through the bayʿah, the pledge of allegiance by which the community expresses its consent and commitment to the chosen leader. These abyāt define it, set out the conditions of a valid bayʿah and how many must give it, and hold that one Imām leads all the Muslims, for life, unless necessity rules otherwise.

verses.tr: The bayʿah is a pledge of acceptance clear. And obedience to the chosen leader is sincere.

exp.en:
Once the Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd have reached their decision and identified the most suitable candidate for Imāmah, the next step is to formalize that leadership. This is done through the bayʿah, the pledge of allegiance, by which the community expresses its consent and commitment to the chosen leader.

Definition: the bayʿah is a public act of showing consent and obedience to the Imām; it represents the willingness of the people to obey the Imām and support him in governing according to the Sharīʿah.

Linguistically, the term comes from bayʿ (a transaction), because both involve a form of mutual agreement. It is named after the act of “selling” because, in a sale, each party extends their hand: the seller delivers the goods, and the buyer receives them. So the name reflects the mutual pledge or commitment.

The traditional handshake is symbolic, not essential; what counts is genuine consent and readiness to follow. Those near him are recommended to express it by hand, while others may convey it verbally or through acknowledgment. What matters is the intent to accept his authority and the public recognition of his position.

verses.tr: Their pledge is due to the worthiest first, then the next in line, he should accept it, and to the first pledge, remain true and confined.

exp.en:
Conditions for a valid bayʿah

A valid bayʿah rests on three foundational conditions:

  1. Choosing the most suitable candidate. The pledge should be given to the most qualified individual available (al-amthal fa-al-amthal). If an ideal candidate is not possible, the most capable under the circumstances is chosen, balancing qualities such as knowledge, strength, and popular acceptance.
  2. Acceptance by the Imām. Since bayʿah is an act of offer and acceptance, it only takes effect when the chosen person agrees to assume responsibility. In exceptional cases where refusal would cause chaos, and there is no other alternative, scholars allow compulsion to preserve unity.
    Should the selected individual decline the offer, and another eligible candidate exists, the bayʿah becomes invalid, and Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd must select the next best available option.
  3. Respecting the first valid bayʿah. Once an Imām is rightfully established, a second pledge to another person is invalid. The Prophet ﷺ said, “Fulfill the bayʿah of the first and give them their rights,” emphasizing that duplicating allegiance only breeds division.
    If two bayʿahs are made unintentionally, such as in the case of being unaware of an existing valid pledge, the first bayʿah remains binding, while the second is considered void. The primary objective is to maintain harmony and avert conflict.

verses.tr: Five suffice - three with two agree, and one may bind the rule legally.

exp.en:
Number required to appoint the Imām

Classical scholars offered varying views on how many people must give the pledge for it to be legitimate:

  • Five persons based on ʿUmar’s six-man council.
  • Three persons analogous to a marriage contract.
  • Two persons similar to a sale agreement.
  • One person a sole authorized representative.
  • A sufficient number requires enough qualified individuals for unity.

First opinion: five persons. Some scholars held that at least five qualified persons are needed. They based this on the precedent of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, who made the matter of succession a shūrā (consultative council) among six Companions, instructing that five would choose one. The caliphate of ʿUthmān رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ was established through the agreement of five of these Companions: ʿAlī, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, Ṭalḥah, and al-Zubayr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ.

Hence, they deduced that the minimum number required to make the appointment binding is five.

Second opinion: three persons. Others said three are sufficient, by analogy with the marriage contract, which is valid with a walī and two witnesses. Just as that is a binding contract, the bayʿah too would be binding with three.

Third opinion: two persons. A third group argued that two are enough, like a contract of sale, which only requires two parties: one making the offer and the other accepting. Also, because two is the minimum form of plural (jamʿ) in Arabic, and congregation (jamāʿah) in prayer is valid with two.

Fourth opinion: one person. Some scholars argued that even one qualified person may establish the Imāmah, citing the example of the pledge of ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ to Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ at Saqīfah. They also compared it to the case of designation by a previous ruler (istikhlāf), where the caliphate is valid through the decision of one predecessor.

verses.tr: Some say the rule is rightly begun only if the majority of ahl al-ḥall approve as one.

exp.en:
Fifth opinion: the majority view. Most scholars (jumhūr), including Ibn Taymiyyah, Abū Yaʿlā, and Imām al-Juwaynī, held that:

The Imāmah does not validly form by the pledge of one, two, three, or even five persons; rather, it is established by the general agreement of the Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd, those who possess real influence and authority in the Ummah.

This is the most widely accepted view: that the bayʿah becomes binding once enough qualified individuals give their consent, so that the leader gains real authority and the Ummah’s unity is secured.

They argue that the pledge of ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ to Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ did not become binding merely through that initial act. It only became binding when most of the Companions expressed their approval and gave their bayʿah. Similarly, in the appointment of ʿUthmān رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, it was not the five alone, but the broad acceptance of the Ṣaḥābah, including the Muhājirūn, Anṣār, and the commanders of the armies.

As Ibn Taymiyyah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ explained:

“A man does not become an Imām merely through a pledge by a few. He becomes an Imām only when those with real authority (ahl al-qudrah wa al-shawkah) pledge to him. The appointment of Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ became valid when the Companions accepted and obeyed him. Had they refused, he would not have become Imām.”

Thus, the Imāmate is validated by broad public acknowledgment and support, ensuring the Imām’s power, authority, and ability to govern.

verses.tr: With this pledge, the rule is confirmed, and all thereafter to him are turned.

exp.en:
The bayʿah and its types

  • Bayʿat al-Inʿiqād (constitutive bayʿah): This is the pledge given by the Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd, the qualified scholars, leaders, and representatives of the community who have the authority to appoint an Imām. When these people give their pledge, the Imāmate is formally established for that leader.
  • Bayʿat al-ʿĀmmah (public bayʿah): After the Imāmate has been established through the Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd, the rest of the Muslims follow with their general pledge, which means showing acceptance, satisfaction, and obedience to that Imām.

Bayʿat al-Inʿiqād: the formal pledge → Bayʿat al-ʿĀmmah: widespread acceptance

Thus, when the Prophet ﷺ said, “Whoever dies without a pledge (of allegiance) on his neck dies a death of ignorance (jāhiliyyah),” it does not mean that every single person must personally go to the Imām and physically pledge to him. Rather, the meaning is that once the Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd have pledged and the Imāmate has been validly established, every Muslim must recognize and obey that Imām, as this is what constitutes the general pledge (Bayʿat al-ʿĀmmah).

verses.tr: One leader governs all the earth, until necessity brings new birth.

exp.en:
The ruling on having multiple Imāms

The majority of Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jamāʿah hold that it is not permissible to have multiple Imāms in the same period, even if the Muslim lands cover the entire globe (al-maʿmūrah, meaning all inhabited regions of the earth).

The principle is that the whole Muslim world should be united under one Imām, whose leadership brings together the word of the Muslims, just as it was during the time of the Prophet ﷺ and then his rightly guided successors (al-Khulafāʾ al-Rāshidūn), who were single caliphs for all Muslims across the earth.

The Prophet ﷺ said:

إِذَا بُويِعَ لِخَلِيفَتَيْنِ، فَاقْتُلُوا الْآخَرَ مِنْهُمَا

“If two caliphs are given allegiance, then kill the latter of the two.” Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim

This ḥadīth makes clear that only one legitimate Imām can exist at a time.

The second opinion: Some scholars, such as Imām al-Ḥaramayn al-Juwaynī, who attributed this view to Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī, al-Isfarāyinī, and the mufassir al-Qurṭubī, allowed for the permissibility of multiple Imāms in different lands, out of necessity.

They argued that when the Muslim territories become vast and distant, and it becomes impossible for one ruler to manage all affairs, it is permissible for separate Imāms to govern different regions, each maintaining justice within their domain.

Historical context: When Sayyidunā ʿAlī and Muʿāwiyah رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا were both leading different regions, Muʿāwiyah had not been pledged allegiance as a caliph; he was simply governing Shām (Syria). Only after the martyrdom of ʿAlī did Muʿāwiyah receive bayʿah as caliph.

When al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ succeeded his father, he later ceded the caliphate to Muʿāwiyah رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ for the sake of unity, and the Ummah once again gathered under a single Imām.

Later, during the time of ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Zubayr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, there were again two rulers, Ibn al-Zubayr in Makkah and ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān in Syria, until unity was restored when Ibn ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ and the rest of the Muslims gave allegiance to ʿAbd al-Malik.

Then, from the Abbasid period onward, a practical division occurred: the Abbasid caliphs ruled over the eastern Islamic world, while the Umayyads established a separate rule in al-Andalus (Spain). From that time, in the 2nd century AH, two caliphs existed simultaneously: a historical reality, though contrary to the ideal principle.

Duration and limit of the Imāmate

The Imāmate, by its original sharʿī principle, is permanent (muʾabbad), meaning the Imām remains in office until death or valid removal. Just as the Imām’s authority is not geographically limited, it was also not time-limited.

Example: The early caliphs remained in office until they passed away or were removed for a legitimate reason.

In modern political systems, however, leadership terms are limited, for example to four, five, or six years, depending on the constitution of each state. This type of time-restricted bayʿah is a modern ijtihād (legal reasoning) developed by contemporary scholars.

They based it on analogy: just as earlier jurists permitted limiting the Imāmate geographically (for example, an Imām appointed over one country or province rather than the entire Muslim world), so too it is permissible to limit it by time, making the leader’s authority valid for a defined period. After this term, the bayʿah can either be renewed or transferred to another person.

So, the necessity applies to both issues:

  1. The unity of the Imāmate: one ruler for all lands.
  2. The permanent nature of his rule.

In times of necessity, exceptions can be made for multiple leaders or time-bound terms.

Modern leaders and the classical conditions

Modern presidents, kings, and emirs do not carry the full authority of a sharʿī Caliph (Khalīfah). Therefore, the classical conditions, such as being Qurashī (from Quraysh), are not applied to them. Each state organizes its leadership and bayʿah according to its own system, as agreed upon by its Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd.

chapters.desc: After the appointment and the pledge of allegiance, the next important question is: when can a Khalīfah be removed from office? The Imāmah is a sacred trust, not a personal right; just as it is bound by conditions at the start, it remains bound by those same conditions throughout.

verses.tr: His removal comes by apostasy or madness plain, captivity or sin that brings disdain.

exp.en:
After the appointment and pledge of allegiance (bayʿah), the next important question is: when can a Khalīfah be removed from office?

The Imāmah is a sacred trust, not a personal right. Just as it is bound by conditions at the start, it remains bound by those same conditions throughout.

When these are violated or lost, the legitimacy of the Imāmah is affected, and it becomes the duty of Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd to assess, deliberate, and decide.

The causes of dismissal are five:

  1. Apostasy (al-riddah)
  2. Insanity (al-junūn)
  3. Captivity (al-asr)
  4. Open sinfulness (al-fisq)
  5. Voluntary resignation (khalʿu nafsihi)

And to these, scholars add a general principle: any condition that was required for his appointment, if it no longer exists, the Imāmah no longer stands.

1. Apostasy (al-riddah)

Islam is the foundation of the Imāmah. If faith is lost, authority collapses. The Qurʾān states:

﴿وَلَنْ يَجْعَلَ اللَّهُ لِلْكَافِرِينَ عَلَى الْمُؤْمِنِينَ سَبِيلًا﴾

“And Allah will never grant the disbelievers authority over the believers.” al-Nisāʾ 4:141

The Prophet ﷺ said:

وَأَنْ لَا نُنَازِعَ الْأَمْرَ أَهْلَهُ، إِلَّا أَنْ تَرَوْا كُفْرًا بَوَاحًا عِنْدَكُمْ مِنَ اللَّهِ فِيهِ بُرْهَانٌ

“Do not dispute with those in authority unless you see open disbelief for which you have clear proof from Allah.” al-Bukhārī and Muslim

Ibn Ḥajar رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ explains:

“He is removed from leadership by disbelief, unanimously.”

Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ states: “The scholars have agreed that the Imāmah does not belong to a disbeliever; and if disbelief occurs, he is automatically deposed.”

However, it is important to note that if the ruler apostatises and the Muslims lack the strength to depose him, remaining under his control is tolerated out of necessity, to preserve life, order, and public safety.

But if the Muslims possess the strength and unity to replace him with a believing leader, then removing him becomes a duty of Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd.

2. Insanity (al-junūn)

Leadership demands sound reason. If the Khalīfah permanently loses his mind, through insanity, coma, or a condition that removes awareness, he is removed from office.

But if the condition is temporary or occasional, scholars differ:

  • Some hold that even intermittent loss of reason invalidates leadership.
  • Others maintain that as long as the leader regains awareness and is capable most of the time, his Imāmah remains valid.

The guiding principle is: if his mental state prevents him from governance, his Imāmah cannot stand.

3. Captivity (al-asr)

When a Khalīfah is captured, the ruling depends on circumstances.

If captured by disbelievers:

  • If there is hope of rescue, he remains the Imām. A deputy is appointed temporarily to manage affairs until his release.
  • If there is no hope of release, he is considered deposed, and a new Imām is appointed.

If captured by Muslim rebels (bughāh):

  • If rescue is possible, he remains the Imām.
  • If not, and the rebels have no organised authority, his Imāmah continues, and a deputy is appointed temporarily to manage affairs until his release.
  • But if the rebels establish their own ruler and territory, the first Imām is considered removed, and a new one must be appointed.

If later freed, he does not return to leadership once another valid Imām has been appointed.

4. Open sinfulness (al-fisq)

This is the most debated cause. The Khalīfah is not removed for every personal sin, but when sin undermines the purpose of the Imāmah itself.

Scholars divide fisq into two levels:

(a) Personal fisq: sins that harm the ruler himself (like drinking, zinā, or neglecting prayer), while he still rules by justice and protects the people. Most scholars hold that this does not automatically nullify his Imāmah, though it is reprehensible and sinful.

(b) Public fisq: injustice or corruption that harms the community: oppression, bloodshed, spreading immorality, or suspending the Sharīʿah. This fisq invalidates the Imāmah, because it destroys the very purpose of leadership.

Hence, the scholars have three positions:

  1. No removal at all for fisq: it is a condition at appointment, not for continuation.
  2. Automatic removal for any fisq: any fisq justifies immediate removal.
  3. Distinction: only that which affects the Ummah’s religion and safety justifies removal.

This third view is the most balanced and widely accepted.

verses.tr: The just may depose for flagrant wrong, or he may step down of his own accord along.

exp.en:
On removal for fisq, which the poet assigns to Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd, Imām al-Qurṭubī said:

“If the Imām becomes manifestly corrupt and unjust, his Imāmah dissolves, for his purpose, to uphold justice, is lost.”

Imām al-Shawkānī added:

“If removal can be done without bloodshed, it is obligatory; if not, patience becomes the duty.”

Thus, Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd must weigh the harms: if deposing him causes greater chaos, restraint becomes wiser. The goal is always to preserve unity and prevent greater fitnah.

5. Voluntary resignation (khalʿu nafsihi)

A Khalīfah may step down voluntarily, but only under specific conditions.

Historical context: The Prophet’s Companions discussed this when Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ initially offered to withdraw, saying, “Release me from this pledge.” ʿAlī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ replied, “We will not release you, nor will we accept your withdrawal. The Messenger of Allah placed you ahead of us; who then could dare to set you aside?”

ʿUthmān رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ refused to step down under pressure, saying:

“I will not remove the garment that Allah has clothed me with.”

But al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ abdicated willingly, reconciling the divided Ummah and fulfilling the prophecy of the Prophet ﷺ: “This son of mine is a leader. Through him, Allah will reconcile two great groups of Muslims.”

Imām al-Qurṭubī said:

“It is obligatory for him to resign if he finds in himself a deficiency that prevents him from fulfilling the role.”

Imām al-Juwaynī added:

“And if the Imām realizes that stepping down will not harm the Muslims, but instead will extinguish a blazing conflict, prevent widespread conflict, spare blood from being shed, and relieve the Muslim community from hardship and exhaustion, then there is no harm in him resigning from his position.

“This was precisely the case of al-Ḥasan (may Allah be pleased with him), whose abdication the Prophet ﷺ had foretold when al-Ḥasan was still a young child. The Prophet would place his hand on his head and say: ‘This son of mine is a leader, and through him Allah will bring peace between two great groups of Muslims.’”

So, if abdication serves the Ummah’s interest, whether to avoid conflict, restore unity, or protect faith, it is valid. But if it springs from personal weariness or worldly motives, Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd may reject it.

The matter always returns to public interest (maṣlaḥah) and collective judgment.

chapters.desc: The poet seals his work with reverence and praise, turning hearts back to the Messenger of Allah, who embodied perfect leadership in both spirit and law, and then praises Allah and hides the number of his verses in a single word. The book’s conclusion and its glossary of terms close the commentary.

verses.tr: I end with prayers and peace sublime, upon the Prophet, merciful and kind.

exp.en:
With this, the discussion of the Imāmate reaches its conclusion: a topic that has borne the weight of governance, justice, and faith throughout Islamic history. From the conditions of appointment to the causes of removal, each principle reflects the deep concern of scholars to preserve the moral and legal soundness of leadership in the Ummah.

The Imām’s position is not one of privilege but of responsibility; his rise and fall are bound by the same divine ethics that guide every believer.

The poet seals his work beautifully with reverence and praise, turning hearts back to the one who embodied perfect leadership in both spirit and law: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. His compassion and mercy are the true measure of all authority, and his example remains the highest model for any who lead or are led.

verses.tr: Its verses are 43 — the count is known — and praise be to Allah, by Whom it’s done.

exp.en:
The author concludes by praising Allah, declaring that the manẓūmah (poem) is now complete. He then gives a clue to the number of verses using the word جَمٌّ.

جَمٌّ Abundant, many

Literally, جَمٌّ means abundant or many, but here the author uses it with a tawriyah (double entendre).

What is tawriyah? Tawriyah means a word has two meanings:

  • One that is close to the mind but not intended (here, “many”).
  • Another that is farther but intended (the numerical value).

So, while جَمٌّ appears to mean “many”, the author actually hints at a number through the abjad system.

The abjad system

In classical Arabic, every letter has a numerical value. The eastern arrangement is:

أبجد هوز حطي كلمن سعفص قرشت ثخذ ضظغ

  • أ Alif: 1
  • ب Bāʾ: 2
  • ج Jīm: 3
  • د Dāl: 4
  • ه Hāʾ: 5
  • و Wāw: 6
  • ز Zāy: 7
  • ح Ḥāʾ: 8
  • ط Ṭāʾ: 9
  • ي Yāʾ: 10
  • ك Kāf: 20
  • ل Lām: 30
  • م Mīm: 40
  • ن Nūn: 50
  • س Sīn: 60
  • ع ʿAyn: 70
  • ف Fāʾ: 80
  • ص Ṣād: 90
  • ق Qāf: 100
  • ر Rāʾ: 200
  • ش Shīn: 300
  • ت Tāʾ: 400
  • ث Thāʾ: 500
  • خ Khāʾ: 600
  • ذ Dhāl: 700
  • ض Ḍād: 800
  • ظ Ẓāʾ: 900
  • غ Ghayn: 1000

So:

  • ج = 3
  • م = 40

Together = 43. Thus, جَمّ indicates that the poem contains 43 verses.

Conclusion

This work, al-Siyāsah al-Sharʿiyyah, represents not only a profound study of Islamic governance, leadership, and the principles of allegiance (bayʿah), but also a unique insight into the thought of its author, Shaykh Waleed Idris al-Meneese. This was but an attempt to produce a concise overview and translation of the original text, capturing its essential meanings while retaining its scholarly and poetic tone.

The translation of this work was undertaken to prepare for the reading of this poem to my teacher, Shaykh Ismāʿīl Londt, for ijāzah, and equally to make this knowledge accessible to those who do not read or understand Arabic. It is hoped that this translation bridges the gap between classical Islamic scholarship and contemporary seekers of knowledge, allowing both students and scholars to benefit from the wisdom embedded within these lines.

May Allah grant that this work serves as a means of understanding, reflection, and guidance, and may it inspire all who engage with it to pursue knowledge with sincerity, humility, and dedication to the service of the Muslim community.

Glossary

  • Al-Imām – The leader or ruler of the Muslim community; the one who holds authority over the affairs of Muslims according to the Sharīʿah.
  • Al-Bayʿah – Oath of allegiance to the Imām. There are two types:
    • Bayʿat al-Inʿiqād – The formal pledge by the people of authority, Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd, that establishes the Imām’s legitimacy.
    • Bayʿat al-ʿĀmmah – The general pledge of the people showing satisfaction and obedience to the Imām after the formal pledge.
  • Ahl al-Ḥall wa al-ʿAqd – People of knowledge, authority, and responsibility who have the power to appoint or remove an Imām.
  • Al-Maʿmūrah – Literally “the inhabited world”; in this context, it refers to all Muslim lands under the Imām’s authority.
  • Al-ʿAzl – Removal or dismissal of the Imām from his position for valid reasons.
  • Al-Fisq – Open sinful behavior or disobedience that may compromise the Imām’s authority or the welfare of the community.
  • Al-Riddah – Apostasy; the renunciation of Islam by the Imām, which necessitates his removal.
  • Al-Junūn – Permanent insanity or incapacity that renders the Imām unable to fulfill his duties.
  • Al-Asr – Captivity; if the Imām is captured and cannot govern effectively, rules exist for delegation or removal.
  • Khalʿ al-Nafs – Voluntary resignation of the Imām from leadership for personal, religious, or worldly reasons.
  • Al-Ijmāʿ – Consensus of scholars on a particular ruling; sometimes cited in debates about leadership and legitimacy.
  • Al-Tawriyah – A rhetorical device in Arabic poetry where a word or phrase carries two meanings: the apparent (literal) and the intended (hidden).
  • Al-Jumm – In abjad numerology, it refers to the total numerical value of letters in a word or phrase, often used to calculate poetic or textual significance.
  • Abjad system – Arabic letter-number system where each letter corresponds to a numerical value, used in literary, poetic, and scholarly calculations.
